name: Petzl Voltige Chest Harness
title: Petzl Voltige Chest Harness for Tree Climbing
meta: The Petzl Voltige chest harness adds shoulder straps to a seat harness to keep you upright and spread the weight of a loaded saddle. Fit, use, and price.
tagline: A light chest harness that pairs with a seat harness for upright, balanced climbing.
summary: The Petzl Voltige chest harness is a lightweight set of shoulder straps that connects to a seat harness to help hold your upper body upright. Climbers use it to take some of the gear weight off the hips and to keep a chest-mounted device or rope in a tidy position.
highlights: Lightweight shoulder straps for use with a seat harness
Helps keep the upper body upright on long ascents
Shares the load of a heavy gear setup between hips and shoulders
Adjustable to fit over a jacket or a T-shirt
specs: No (positioning and comfort only, unless the manufacturer states otherwise)

body.h: What the Voltige does on a climb
p: A full saddle loaded with a saw, handsaw, rigging gear, and a couple of lanyards pulls down and back on your hips. Shoulder straps spread some of that weight onto your upper body, so the saddle sits where it should and you are not constantly hitching it up between cuts.

Straps like the Voltige also help on long rope ascents. They keep your torso closer to the rope, which makes footlocking or a chest-mounted ascender feel more efficient, and they give you a tidy place to route a rope or tool tether. Look for strap length and buckle adjustment that let it fit over winter layers as well as a shirt.

Check that the chest harness is compatible with your seat harness before you buy, and that the connection points line up without twisting. Petzl publishes compatibility notes and connection instructions; follow them, and browse other saddle parts and shoulder harnesses if you run a different saddle.

Treat chest straps as a positioning and comfort accessory unless the manufacturer specifically rates the connection for something more. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is the Petzl Voltige a full-body harness?
faq.a: No. It is a chest harness that works together with a seat harness. Use it only in the configurations Petzl's instructions describe.

faq.q: Why would an arborist wear a chest harness?
faq.a: It helps carry the weight of a loaded saddle, keeps you upright during long ascents, and can hold a chest ascender or rope in position.

name: Teufelberger treeMOTION ANSI Spare Bridge
title: Teufelberger treeMOTION ANSI Spare Bridge
meta: A treeMOTION ANSI spare bridge replaces the worn rope bridge on Teufelberger's ANSI saddle. Learn when to swap it, how to inspect it, and what it costs.
tagline: Factory replacement bridge for the ANSI version of the Teufelberger treeMOTION saddle.
summary: This treeMOTION ANSI spare bridge is the factory replacement rope bridge for the ANSI version of the Teufelberger treeMOTION saddle. The bridge is the main attachment point on the saddle and wears faster than anything else on it, so most climbers keep a spare on hand.
highlights: Replacement bridge for the treeMOTION ANSI saddle
Bridge is a wear item and should be replaced on schedule
Keeps your saddle in service without waiting on parts
Fit to the saddle version it is made for

p: Every move you make in the tree runs through the bridge. Your rope connector or ring slides back and forth on it all day, and the abrasion, sap, and grit add up. That is why Teufelberger designs it as a replaceable part rather than sewing it into the saddle.

Inspect the bridge before every climb. Look for fuzzing, glazing, flat spots, cuts, or a stiff section where the connector rides. If you find damage, or the bridge has reached the service life in Teufelberger's instructions, retire it and install a new one.

Keep the spare in a clean, dry bag away from fuel, bar oil, and sunlight so it is in good shape when you need it. Write the install date on your gear log so you can track how long each bridge lasts on your saddle; that tells you how often to reorder.

treeMOTION saddles have been made in different versions over the years, and bridges are not always interchangeable. Confirm that this spare matches the ANSI version of your saddle and the bridge length you run, then install it exactly as the instructions show, including the stopper knots or terminations. You can find other saddle parts in the same section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: How often should I replace a treeMOTION bridge?
faq.a: Replace it when inspection shows wear or damage, or when it reaches the service life in Teufelberger's instructions, whichever comes first. Busy climbers often swap bridges several times over the life of a saddle.

faq.q: Will this bridge fit a treeMOTION evo?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Match the bridge to your exact saddle model and version and check Teufelberger's parts information before ordering.

name: Teufelberger treeMOTION evo Knotted Rope Bridge
title: treeMOTION evo Knotted Rope Bridge Replacement
h1: Teufelberger treeMOTION evo Knotted Rope Bridge
meta: The treeMOTION evo knotted rope bridge is Teufelberger's replacement bridge for the evo saddle. See how it installs, how to inspect it, and when to retire it.
tagline: Knotted rope replacement bridge for the Teufelberger treeMOTION evo saddle.
summary: The treeMOTION evo knotted rope bridge is a replacement rope bridge with knotted terminations for Teufelberger's treeMOTION evo saddle. It lets you swap out a worn bridge yourself and keep the saddle working.
highlights: Replacement rope bridge for the treeMOTION evo
Knotted terminations for installation on the saddle
Bridge is a wear part; swap it when inspection calls for it
Good spare to keep in the truck

p: The bridge on a treeMOTION evo carries your climbing system, your lanyard connections, and often a rope wrench or device tether. It rubs against hardware all day, so it is designed to be replaced long before the rest of the saddle is worn out.

A knotted bridge is installed by threading it through the saddle's bridge attachment points and finishing it with the stopper knots Teufelberger specifies. Dress the knots tight, check the length is correct, and load-test the setup low before you leave the ground. If the instructions call for a specific knot or tail length, follow them exactly.

Bridge length changes how your saddle works. A longer bridge gives more side-to-side reach and lets a rope wrench or device ride further from your body; a shorter one keeps everything tight and close. If you are unsure what length you run now, measure the old bridge before you cut it off, and keep your setup consistent.

Check the bridge before each climb for cuts, glazing, flattened or stiff sections, and slipped knots. Retire it at the first sign of damage. Keeping a spare in your gear bag means one worn bridge does not end a work week. Browse more treeMOTION parts and shoulder harnesses here.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I tie my own replacement bridge?
faq.a: Use the bridge and termination method Teufelberger approves for your saddle. A home-made bridge may not meet the saddle's certification.

faq.q: Does it fit the original treeMOTION?
faq.a: This bridge is made for the evo. Check Teufelberger's parts chart if you run an earlier treeMOTION.

name: Teufelberger treeMOTION evo Rope Bones
title: Teufelberger treeMOTION evo Rope Bones
meta: treeMOTION evo rope bones are a Teufelberger accessory for the evo saddle. See what they do, how to check fit with your setup, and how to inspect them.
tagline: A rope-based accessory part for configuring the Teufelberger treeMOTION evo saddle.
summary: The treeMOTION evo rope bones are a rope-based accessory from Teufelberger made to fit the treeMOTION evo saddle. Climbers use them to set up attachment points on the saddle the way they want them.
highlights: Made for the Teufelberger treeMOTION evo
Lets you customize how the saddle is set up
Install and use only as the manufacturer describes

body.h: Setting up an evo your way
p: Part of the appeal of the treeMOTION evo is how far you can configure it. Bridges, connection points, and gear-carrying options can be changed to suit an SRS climber, a hitch climber, or someone who spends most days on spurs doing removals. Rope bones are one of the parts Teufelberger offers for that kind of tuning.

Before you buy, read Teufelberger's description and instructions for the rope bones and confirm how they attach and what they are meant to hold. Some saddle accessories are life-support components and some are for gear carrying only. Never load a part beyond the role the manufacturer gives it.

If you are unsure whether rope bones suit your setup, compare them with the parts already on your saddle and talk with someone who runs the same evo configuration. Mixing parts from different saddle versions is a common source of fit problems.

Treat rope saddle parts like any other textile in your kit. Check for cuts, fuzzing, glazing, chemical contamination, and stiff sections before each climb, keep them away from bar oil and fuel, and retire them when they are worn. More saddle parts for the treeMOTION are listed in this category.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Do rope bones fit the original treeMOTION?
faq.a: They are listed for the treeMOTION evo. Check Teufelberger's parts information before using them on any other saddle.

faq.q: Are rope bones life-support equipment?
faq.a: Follow the manufacturer's instructions for how the part may be loaded. Do not use any saddle accessory for life support unless the instructions say you can.

name: Teufelberger treeMOTION Shoulder Straps
title: Teufelberger treeMOTION Shoulder Straps
meta: treeMOTION shoulder straps take the weight of a loaded saddle off your hips and keep it in place. See fit, setup tips, and the typical price of this add-on.
tagline: Add-on shoulder straps that carry part of a loaded treeMOTION saddle's weight.
summary: treeMOTION shoulder straps clip onto Teufelberger's treeMOTION saddle to carry some of its weight on your shoulders. With a saw, handsaw, and rigging gear hanging off the saddle, the straps keep it from sagging and make long days easier on your hips.
highlights: Made to attach to the Teufelberger treeMOTION
Moves part of the gear load onto your shoulders
Keeps the saddle sitting where it should
Adjustable to fit over different layers

p: A treeMOTION already carries weight well, but a full rack still pulls down on your hips. Saw on one side, handsaw and pole saw on the other, a lanyard, a few slings and carabiners: by midafternoon you feel it. Shoulder straps transfer part of that load to your upper body and keep the waist belt from creeping down.
Straps also help when you are hanging in the saddle on a long ascent or working out on a limb, because the saddle stays oriented and the attachment points stay where your hands expect them.

Straps are also handy for climbers who run a chest-mounted ascender or a rope-walking setup on SRS, because they keep the chest attachment in position. Check that your system is set up the way the device and saddle manufacturers describe.

Attach the straps at the points Teufelberger specifies and adjust them so they are snug without pulling the saddle up into your ribs. Check the adjustment again over a winter jacket. Confirm the straps match your treeMOTION version; other saddle parts and shoulder harnesses are listed in this category.

Shoulder straps are a comfort and positioning accessory, not a substitute for your saddle's rated attachment points. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Do the straps fit the treeMOTION evo?
faq.a: Check Teufelberger's compatibility information for your exact saddle version before ordering.

faq.q: Can I clip my lanyard to the shoulder straps?
faq.a: No. Connect life-support gear only to the saddle's rated attachment points.

name: Teufelberger Webbing Bridge
title: Teufelberger Webbing Bridge for treeMOTION Saddles
meta: The Teufelberger webbing bridge is a flat textile option for the treeMOTION saddle. Compare it with a rope bridge and learn how to inspect and replace it.
tagline: Flat webbing bridge option for Teufelberger treeMOTION saddles.
summary: The Teufelberger webbing bridge is a flat textile bridge made for Teufelberger's treeMOTION saddles. Some climbers prefer webbing to a round rope bridge for the way a ring or connector rides on it.
highlights: Webbing alternative to a rope bridge
Different feel for rings and connectors sliding on it

p: Rope bridges are the most common choice, but a webbing bridge has a different feel. A flat bridge spreads contact across a wider surface, and some climbers find a ring or carabiner tracks along it differently than on round rope. Others simply want a spare that matches what came on their saddle.
Whatever you choose, the bridge is the part that takes the most wear on a saddle. It is designed to be replaced, so keep a spare and do not try to stretch the life of a worn one.

Webbing is also easy to inspect: cuts and abrasion show clearly across the flat surface. If you run a ring on the bridge, check where the ring sits all day, since that is usually where wear shows up first. Keep a spare in the truck, stored dry and away from fuel and oil.

Make sure the bridge matches your treeMOTION model and version, then install it exactly as Teufelberger shows. Before each climb, look for cuts, abrasion through the weave, glazing, stiff spots, and damaged stitching. Retire it at the first sign of damage. Other saddle parts are listed in this category.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is a webbing bridge stronger than a rope bridge?
faq.a: Both are designed to meet the saddle's requirements when installed correctly. Choose based on feel and compatibility, and follow Teufelberger's instructions.

faq.q: How do I know when to replace it?
faq.a: Replace it when inspection finds damage or wear, or when it reaches the service life in the manufacturer's instructions.

name: Tree Austria Stainless Steel Shackle
title: Tree Austria Stainless Steel Shackle for Saddles
meta: The Tree Austria stainless steel shackle is a compact connector for saddle bridges and fixed attachment points. How arborists use it and what to check first.
tagline: Compact stainless steel shackle for saddle bridge and attachment-point setups.
summary: The Tree Austria stainless steel shackle is a compact shackle climbers use for semi-permanent connections on a saddle, such as at a bridge or fixed attachment point. Stainless steel resists corrosion, and a shackle stays put where a carabiner might rotate.
highlights: Compact shape for saddle and bridge connections
Resists corrosion from sweat and weather

p: Some connections on a saddle do not need to be opened during the day: a bridge termination, a fixed rope-wrench tether, or a ring captured on a bridge. A small shackle is lower profile than a carabiner, it cannot be accidentally opened with a gate, and it will not cross-load the way a carabiner can when it rotates.
Stainless steel holds up to sweat, rain, and sap without rusting, which matters on a part that stays on the saddle for months.

Match the shackle size to the parts it joins. It should fit a bridge eye or ring without forcing the pin, and it should not leave the connection loose enough to cross-load. Keep spares the same size so swaps are straightforward.

Only use a shackle in a life-support position if it is rated and marked for that use and your saddle's instructions allow it. Check the strength markings on the part itself, close the pin fully, and secure it as the manufacturer directs so it cannot back out. Inspect it for wear grooves, cracks, and a bent pin. Other saddle parts are in this category.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Can I use this shackle instead of a carabiner?
faq.a: Only where the shackle's rating and your saddle's instructions allow it. Shackles suit fixed connections that do not need opening during the climb.

faq.q: How do I keep the pin from loosening?
faq.a: Tighten it fully and secure it the way the manufacturer specifies. Check it every time you inspect your saddle.

name: Tree Austria 3.2 Replacement Bridge
title: Tree Austria 3.2 Replacement Bridge for Saddles
meta: The Tree Austria 3.2 replacement bridge keeps your saddle in service when the old bridge wears. Why bridges wear, how to inspect one, and how to swap it.
tagline: Replacement bridge for the Tree Austria 3.2 saddle.
summary: The Tree Austria 3.2 replacement bridge is made for the Tree Austria 3.2 saddle. Bridges are the highest-wear part of a climbing saddle, and replacing one keeps the rest of the saddle in service.
highlights: Replacement bridge for the Tree Austria 3.2
Bridge is a wear item, not a lifetime part
Keep a spare so a worn bridge does not stop work
Install exactly as the manufacturer shows
specs: Worn, damaged, or past its service life

p: Your climbing system, lanyard, and often your rope wrench all connect through the bridge, and the connector slides on it every time you move. That constant friction is why saddle makers treat the bridge as a replaceable part.

Inspect it before each climb. Fuzzing, glazing, cuts, flattened sections, stiff spots, or contamination from fuel and oil all mean it is time to swap it. Follow the service life in the manufacturer's instructions even if the bridge still looks acceptable.

Keep a spare in a clean, dry bag in the truck, away from fuel and bar oil. Many climbers note the install date in a gear log, which shows how long a bridge lasts in their work and when to reorder. When you retire a bridge, cut it so it cannot end up back in service by mistake.

Confirm the part matches your saddle model and version before you order, since bridge lengths and terminations vary. Install it as Tree Austria shows, check the terminations, and test your setup low before climbing. You will find other saddle parts and shoulder harnesses in this category.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Will this bridge fit other saddles?
faq.a: It is made for the Tree Austria 3.2. Do not fit it to another saddle unless the manufacturer approves it.

faq.q: Can I keep using a bridge with light fuzz?
faq.a: Minor surface fuzz can be normal, but compare it with the manufacturer's inspection criteria. When in doubt, replace it.

name: Weaver Cougar Climbing Harness
title: Weaver Cougar Saddle: Climbing Harness Buying Guide
meta: The Weaver Cougar is a traditional American tree climbing saddle with a padded back and side D-rings. See who it suits, how to size it, and what to inspect.
tagline: A traditional American-style climbing saddle for everyday tree work.
summary: The Weaver Cougar saddle is a traditional American-style tree climbing harness built for everyday pruning and removal work. It uses a padded back with side D-rings and leg straps, the layout a lot of climbers learned on.
highlights: Side D-rings for lanyard and climbing line connections
Tool and gear loops for a working rack

body.h: How the Cougar works on the job
p: American-style saddles like the Cougar keep things simple: a wide padded back, a pair of side D-rings, and leg straps. You clip your flipline across the D-rings for spur work, and you tie in at the D-rings or a bridge setup for climbing on a rope. Many climbers on removal crews still prefer this style because it is easy to check and quick to put on.

Gear loops around the belt carry a handsaw, a few slings, and carabiners. On a long pruning day you may want more leg support than a basic D-ring saddle gives, which is where a seat option like the Cougar with batten seat comes in.

A traditional D-ring saddle is also a good teaching saddle. New climbers can see every connection at a glance, and crew leaders can check a setup quickly from the ground. If you plan to add a rope bridge or ring later, confirm with Weaver which modifications the saddle allows.

Size by waist measurement with the clothes you will climb in, and check the leg straps fit snugly without pinching. Before every climb, inspect stitching, webbing, buckles, and D-rings for wear, cuts, or corrosion.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Is the Weaver Cougar good for spur work?
faq.a: Yes. The side D-ring layout is a common setup for flipline work on removals.

faq.q: Can I use it for SRS?
faq.a: Check Weaver's instructions for approved attachment points and configurations before setting up any SRS system on it.

name: Weaver Cougar Saddle with Batten Seat
keyword: weaver cougar saddle with batten seat
title: Weaver Cougar Saddle with Batten Seat
h1: Weaver Cougar Saddle with Batten Seat
meta: The Weaver Cougar saddle with batten seat adds a supportive seat to a classic climbing harness for long hours aloft. See fit, comfort, and inspection tips.
tagline: The classic Weaver Cougar saddle with a batten seat for long hours in the tree.
summary: The Weaver Cougar saddle with batten seat pairs the traditional Cougar climbing harness with a stiffened seat that you can sit into while working. The seat spreads your weight across the back of the thighs instead of concentrating it on the leg straps.
highlights: Classic Cougar saddle layout with side D-rings
Batten seat for support during long stays aloft
Gear loops for a full working rack
Good choice for climbers who hang in the saddle for hours

p: If you spend most of the day hanging in your saddle, such as pruning large spreading trees or setting rigging, leg straps alone start to dig in. A batten seat uses a stiffened board-like section under the thighs that you can sit back into. It spreads pressure over a wider area and makes it easier to stay in position while you work with both hands.
Everything else is the familiar Cougar layout: padded back, side D-rings, and loops for tools and hardware.

Seat saddles also help when you are cabling, setting up a big rigging point, or pruning a long lead where you have to stay put. Climbers who split their time between spur removals and pruning often keep a seat saddle for the long days and a lighter saddle for quick jobs.

Fit the saddle with the clothes you climb in, then adjust so the seat sits under the thighs without riding up when you lean back. Compare it with other Weaver saddles if you want a different seat or belt style. Inspect webbing, stitching, buckles, and hardware before each climb and retire the saddle if anything is damaged.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Does a batten seat make the saddle heavier?
faq.a: It adds some weight and bulk, but many climbers find the comfort worth it on long days.

faq.q: Is it good for spur removals?
faq.a: Yes, the D-ring layout works with a flipline. Some climbers find a seat less necessary for short removals and more useful on pruning work.

name: Weaver WCL 390 Saddle with Batten Seat
title: Weaver WCL 390 Saddle with Batten Seat
h1: Weaver WCL 390 Saddle with Batten Seat
meta: The Weaver WCL 390 saddle has a batten seat for climbers who spend long hours aloft. See how the seat helps, how to size the saddle, and what to inspect.
tagline: A Weaver climbing saddle with a supportive batten seat for long work positioning.
summary: The Weaver WCL 390 saddle is a Weaver climbing saddle with a batten seat, built for climbers who spend a lot of time sitting in the harness. The stiffened seat supports the thighs and takes pressure off the leg straps during long pruning or rigging jobs.
highlights: Batten seat for comfortable work positioning
Gear loops for saws, slings, and hardware
Made by Weaver, a long-time arborist saddle maker

body.h: Built for time in the tree
p: A batten seat is a stiffened panel that sits under your thighs. When you lean back to make a cut or set a rigging point, you sit into the seat instead of hanging on two narrow leg straps. Over a long day that difference shows up in your legs and lower back.
The WCL 390 keeps the familiar Weaver layout with side D-rings for your flipline and climbing system, and loops around the belt for carrying a handsaw, slings, and carabiners.

Seat saddles shine on cabling and bracing jobs, crown cleaning, and rigging work where you stay in one spot for a long time. On short removal climbs the seat matters less, but many climbers still like having it.

Measure your waist in the clothes you climb in and check Weaver's sizing chart. Adjust so the seat sits under the thighs and the belt rides at the hips. Compare it with the other Weaver saddles to find the belt and seat style you like.

Inspect webbing, stitching, buckles, and D-rings before every climb, and retire the saddle if you find cuts, heavy wear, or damaged hardware. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What is the difference between the WCL 390 and the Cougar with batten seat?
faq.a: Both are Weaver saddles with batten seats. Compare belt construction, padding, and attachment layout in Weaver's specs to pick the one that fits your work.

faq.q: Who is a batten seat saddle for?
faq.a: Climbers who spend long periods sitting in the harness, such as on pruning, cabling, or rigging work.

name: Climb Right Aluminum Climbers with L-Pads
title: Climb Right Aluminum Climbers with L-Pads
h1: Climb Right Aluminum Climbers with L-Pads
meta: Climb Right aluminum climbers with L-pads give removal climbers a light set of spurs with simple, proven pads. See fit tips, gaff care, and the typical price.
tagline: Lightweight aluminum tree climbers fitted with L-shaped pads.
summary: Climb Right Aluminum Climbers with L-Pads pair Climb Right's aluminum climber shanks with L-shaped pads. Aluminum keeps weight down on your legs during long removals, and the pad choice sets how the spurs feel on your calves.
highlights: Aluminum shanks for lighter weight than steel

p: On a big removal you lift your spurs thousands of times. Aluminum shanks cut weight compared with steel, and climbers notice it at the end of the day in their knees and hips. Climb Right builds its aluminum climbers for tree work, with adjustable shanks and tree-length gaffs that can be replaced when worn.

L-shaped pads are the simple, traditional option. They are light, easy to strap on, and many climbers who started on them never switch. If you climb all day, every day, you may want a more supportive pad, but L-pads are a solid place to start.

Set the shank length so the top of the shank sits just below the knee joint and the stirrup fits the arch of your boot. Use a sturdy, supportive boot with a defined heel. Keep gaffs sharp and correctly shaped, and replace them when they are worn or bent. Compare other aluminum spurs if you want a different pad.

Keep gaff guards on whenever the spurs are off your legs, in the truck, or in a gear bag. Sharpen gaffs by hand with a file rather than a grinder, which can overheat the steel, and keep the original profile so the point bites into bark and does not cut out sideways. Buy spare gaffs made for your climbers so a worn set does not sideline you.

Spurs belong on removals and on trees that are coming down, not on trees you are pruning. Inspect gaffs, straps, and pads before each use, follow the manufacturer's instructions, and get proper training before you climb on spikes.

faq.q: Are aluminum climbers as strong as steel?
faq.a: They are built for tree work when used as the manufacturer intends. Steel tends to be heavier and more forgiving of abuse, while aluminum saves weight. Follow Climb Right's instructions and inspect them regularly.

faq.q: Are L-pads comfortable enough for full-time climbing?
faq.a: Many climbers use them every day. Others move to wrap or support pads for more calf and shin support. Try both if you can.

title: Climb Right Aluminum Climbers with T-Pads
h1: Climb Right Aluminum Climbers with T-Pads
meta: Climb Right aluminum climbers with T-pads combine a light spur with simple padded straps for removals. How to fit them, care for gaffs, and what they cost.
